requirements.text: Deny cross-workspace reads and writes; role inheritance and explicit deny have defined precedence.
Revocation races serialize with protected writes; cached decisions cannot silently extend access.
Commit mutations and activity intent atomically; publication is independently retryable.

problem.scope: Authored extension of the canonical workspace-access exercise: enforce tenant/project access during mutations and distinguish committed changes from activity publication. No production authentication is executed.

acceptanceCases.given: A user has edit at epoch 4.
acceptanceCases.then: Reject the stale edit; no mutation or event commits.
acceptanceCases.when: Revoke at epoch 5 before a stale edit commits.

acceptanceCases.given: A mutation commits and a dispatcher crashes.
acceptanceCases.then: One activity record is applied; client success still means only committed mutation.
acceptanceCases.when: Deliver the same outbox ID twice.

acceptanceCases.given: A denied edit and a published activity are recorded in the audit ledger.
acceptanceCases.then: The member is refused; the auditor sees decision reason, policy version and delivery status but not the object's contents.
acceptanceCases.when: A workspace member without audit scope queries the ledger, then an auditor reads it.

evidence.testName: L023 transactional policy denies cross-workspace and explicit deny and replays committed commands before the version check

acceptanceCases.given: Alice has workspace-wide edit with an explicit deny on project P2, Bob belongs to another workspace, and the object is at version 2.
acceptanceCases.then: Bob and the P2 edit are denied; the c1 retry returns its stored committed response at version 3 instead of 409; c2 is stale; the reused c1 is rejected; c3 is denied after revocation; one outbox event exists.
acceptanceCases.when: Bob edits; Alice edits P2; Alice commits c1 on P1, retries c1 with expectedVersion 2, sends c2 with expectedVersion 2 and reuses c1 with other bytes; then her grant is revoked and she sends c3.

stages.explanation: Deny cross-workspace reads and writes; role inheritance and explicit deny have defined precedence. A command binds one authenticated principal, workspace, project, action and commandId; a committed reply means the mutation and its outbox row exist. [Access control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Access_control) decides whether an authenticated identity may perform a particular action. The check must apply to the actual resource and operation, including cached and asynchronous paths.
invariants: A command binds one authenticated principal, workspace, project, action and commandId; a committed reply means the mutation and its outbox row exist.

stages.reason: Deny cross-workspace reads and writes; role inheritance and explicit deny have defined precedence.

stages.explanation: Lock policy and target rows, evaluate inherited grants and explicit deny, then mutate. Own workspace membership, project ancestry, role grants and object rows. Policy rows and the target object are read under one transaction lock; no allow decision is made outside it. [A transaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database_transaction) commits related state changes together or leaves them unapplied. The database must enforce the relevant condition during the write, rather than trusting an earlier read.
invariants: Policy rows and the target object are read under one transaction lock; no allow decision is made outside it.

stages.reason: Lock policy and target rows, evaluate inherited grants and explicit deny, then mutate. Own workspace membership, project ancestry, role grants and object rows.

stages.explanation: Add a tenant/principal/resource/version keyed cache; never cache a private response under a public key. Cache validity is bounded and write authorization is never delegated to a stale entry. [A cache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_replacement_policies) keeps reusable results in limited memory. Eviction controls space, while ownership and invalidation rules determine whether a returned value is still safe to use.
invariants: Cache validity is bounded and write authorization is never delegated to a stale entry.

stages.explanation: Persist an immutable event and the command's stored response under its commandId in the same transaction as the authorized mutation. No event or stored response exists for a rolled-back change, and each commandId has at most one stored response. [Immutable data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable_object) is built as a complete new value rather than changed underneath readers. Publishing one reference lets each reader keep a consistent version.
invariants: No event or stored response exists for a rolled-back change, and each commandId has at most one stored response.

stages.explanation: Claim durable event IDs and retry downstream independently of client success. Queued and published are distinct observable states. [Backoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff) spaces repeated attempts so failures do not create a burst of extra traffic. A retry still needs a stable identity and a clear stopping condition. Consider this case: A mutation commits and a dispatcher crashes. Deliver the same outbox ID twice.
invariants: Queued and published are distinct observable states.

stages.reason: Claim durable event IDs and retry downstream independently of client success.

stages.explanation: Deduplicate event IDs before applying the activity projection. An event ID can affect the projection once. [A queue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queue_%28abstract_data_type%29) separates accepting work from completing it. Capacity, ordering, ownership, and shutdown behavior determine what producers and consumers may safely assume about each item. Consider this case: A mutation commits and a dispatcher crashes. Deliver the same outbox ID twice.
invariants: An event ID can affect the projection once.
stages.question: Can activity be delivered twice?
stages.reason: Deduplicate event IDs before applying the activity projection.
stages.title: Consumer inbox

stages.explanation: Advance policy epoch and serialize protected commits against it; reject stale decisions. Revocation cutoff is the authoritative transaction order. [Replication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Replication_%28computing%29) keeps copies of state on multiple nodes. Copying data alone does not decide which copy may accept writes or how much stale data a read may return. Consider this case: A user has edit at epoch 4.
invariants: Revocation cutoff is the authoritative transaction order.
